overview.what_is_it: An AVL tree is a self-balancing binary search tree where every node's balance factor is -1, 0, or 1.
overview.why_it_matters: It guarantees O(log n) search, insertion, and deletion even for sorted or adversarial input.
overview.core_idea: After each update, climb upward and rotate only where the height difference threatens balance.
overview.time_complexity: Search, insertion, and deletion are O(log n) worst case; each rotation is O(1), and height updates occur along one root-to-leaf path.
overview.space_complexity: O(n) for n stored nodes; O(log n) recursion stack for balanced AVL operations.
when_to_use: In-memory ordered maps or sets needing strict worst-case logarithmic operations
Applications with many lookups and relatively stable data where tighter balance improves search
Systems requiring deterministic performance rather than amortized or probabilistic behavior
common_mistakes: Updating height before returning from recursive insert or delete
Using only balance-factor signs without identifying inner versus outer cases
Forgetting that deletion may require multiple rotations up the ancestor path
Treating any height-balanced tree as an AVL tree without enforcing BST order

real_world_usage.description: In-memory ordered indexes and metadata catalogs can use AVL trees to keep key lookup, insertion, and deletion bounded by O(log n).
Sorted identifiers, scopes, or namespace entries benefit from AVL ordering when deterministic lookup time matters.
Free-block allocators can maintain block addresses in AVL order to find, split, merge, and delete blocks efficiently.

patterns: Maintain ordered keys with guaranteed logarithmic updates
After insert or delete, check imbalance only on the ancestor path
Balance factor outside [-1, 0, 1] implies LL, RR, LR, or RL rotation
constraints: Need guaranteed worst-case O(log n) search and update time
Memory overhead for height or balance-factor fields is acceptable
Duplicate-key policy must be defined before implementation

mcqs.question: What invariant distinguishes an AVL tree from a general binary search tree?
options: Every node has at most two children and an in-order traversal is sorted.
For every node, the heights of the left and right subtrees differ by at most 1.
Every root-to-leaf path has exactly the same length.
Every node's key is greater than both children's keys.
mcqs.answer: For every node, the heights of the left and right subtrees differ by at most 1.
mcqs.hint_teacher: Separate the binary-search-tree ordering invariant from the AVL height-balance invariant.
mcqs.hint_peer: BST keeps keys sorted; AVL also keeps both sides from getting too tall.
mcqs.explanation_teacher: An AVL tree is a binary search tree with an additional invariant: for every node, the height difference between its left and right subtrees is at most 1. A sorted in-order traversal alone describes a BST, not necessarily an AVL tree.
mcqs.explanation_peer: AVL is a BST with a height-checking bodyguard at every node.

mcqs.question: If balance factor is defined as height(left) - height(right), what does a balance factor of -2 at node x indicate?
options: The left subtree is taller than the right subtree by 2.
The right subtree is taller than the left subtree by 2.
Node x is a leaf.
Duplicate keys were inserted under node x.
mcqs.answer: The right subtree is taller than the left subtree by 2.
mcqs.hint_teacher: Use the sign of height(left) - height(right) to identify the heavier side.
mcqs.hint_peer: Negative means the right side is winning the height race.
mcqs.explanation_teacher: A balance factor of -2 means height(left) - height(right) = -2, so the right subtree is two levels taller than the left subtree. This violates the AVL condition and requires rebalancing.
mcqs.explanation_peer: If the number is -2, the right side is too heavy.

mcqs.question: Which rotation fixes an LL imbalance at node z?
options: A single right rotation at z.
A single left rotation at z.
A left rotation followed by a right rotation at z.
No rotation is needed.
mcqs.answer: A single right rotation at z.
mcqs.hint_teacher: LL means the inserted node is in the left subtree of the left child.
mcqs.hint_peer: Left-left means one right turn fixes it.
mcqs.explanation_teacher: In an LL case, the left child of z is left-heavy. A single right rotation around z moves the left child upward and restores the height-balance invariant.
mcqs.explanation_peer: Think of pulling the taller left side up and swinging z down to the right.

mcqs.question: Which rotation sequence fixes an LR imbalance at node z?
options: Left rotate z, then right rotate z.
Left rotate z.left, then right rotate z.
Right rotate z.left, then right rotate z.
Right rotate z.right, then left rotate z.
mcqs.answer: Left rotate z.left, then right rotate z.
mcqs.hint_teacher: LR means the insertion is in the right subtree of the left child, so first convert it to an LL shape.
mcqs.hint_peer: Left-right needs a zig-zag fix: first left, then right.
mcqs.explanation_teacher: For an LR imbalance, the problematic node is in the right subtree of z.left. A left rotation on z.left converts the structure into an LL case, after which a right rotation on z restores balance.
mcqs.explanation_peer: Straighten the bent branch first, then rotate the heavy side up.

mcqs.question: During AVL insertion, why is it sufficient to check and rebalance only the ancestors of the inserted node?
options: Only descendants of the inserted node can change height.
Only the path from the root to the inserted node can have changed subtree heights.
The AVL property applies only to leaves.
The BST property must be checked globally after every insertion.
mcqs.answer: Only the path from the root to the inserted node can have changed subtree heights.
mcqs.hint_teacher: Consider which subtree heights are affected by adding one leaf.
mcqs.hint_peer: Only the road you walked down during insertion feels the change.
mcqs.explanation_teacher: Insertion changes the height of subtrees only along the search path from the root to the new node. Therefore, only ancestors on that path can become imbalanced.
mcqs.explanation_peer: If a node was not on the insertion path, its subtree did not grow.

mcqs.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of insertion in an AVL tree with n nodes?
options: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n log n)
mcqs.hint_teacher: AVL height is logarithmic, and insertion follows one root-to-leaf path plus constant work per level.
mcqs.hint_peer: AVL stays short, so insertion does not scan the whole tree.
mcqs.explanation_teacher: An AVL tree has height O(log n). Insertion descends one path, updates heights on the way back, and performs at most a constant number of rotations at the first imbalanced ancestor, so the total worst-case time is O(log n).
mcqs.explanation_peer: The tree is forced to stay balanced, so the path is short.

mcqs.question: Why can AVL searches perform fewer comparisons than red-black tree searches on the same data?
options: AVL trees are usually more tightly balanced.
AVL trees allow only negative keys.
Red-black trees are not binary trees.
AVL trees do not use comparisons.
mcqs.answer: AVL trees are usually more tightly balanced.
mcqs.hint_teacher: Compare the height bounds and balancing strictness of AVL trees and red-black trees.
mcqs.hint_peer: AVL is the stricter gym coach, so the tree is often shorter.
mcqs.explanation_teacher: Both AVL trees and red-black trees guarantee O(log n) search time, but AVL trees enforce a stricter height balance. This often yields a smaller height and therefore fewer comparisons in successful and unsuccessful searches.
mcqs.explanation_peer: Both are fast, but AVL is usually more tightly trimmed.

mcqs.question: What recurrence gives the minimum number of nodes in an AVL tree of height h, using height(null)=0 and height(single node)=1?
options: h
N(h) = 1 + N(h-1) + N(h-2) for h >= 2, with N(0)=0 and N(1)=1
Fibonacci(h)
mcqs.answer: N(h) = 1 + N(h-1) + N(h-2) for h >= 2, with N(0)=0 and N(1)=1
mcqs.hint_teacher: To minimize nodes at height h while preserving AVL balance, make the two child heights differ by exactly 1.
mcqs.hint_peer: The skinniest AVL tree has one tall child and one slightly shorter child.
mcqs.explanation_teacher: A minimum-size AVL tree of height h has root height h, one child of height h-1, and the other child of height h-2. Thus N(h)=1+N(h-1)+N(h-2), which grows exponentially and implies h=O(log n).
mcqs.explanation_peer: Minimum AVL trees are Fibonacci-shaped, not perfectly full.

mcqs.question: After a right rotation around y, which node becomes the root of the rotated subtree?
options: y
y.left
y.right
The smallest key in y.right
mcqs.hint_teacher: In a right rotation, the left child moves upward.
mcqs.hint_peer: Right rotation means the left kid gets promoted.
mcqs.explanation_teacher: A right rotation around y makes x=y.left the new root of the local subtree. Node y becomes x.right, and x.right's old subtree becomes y.left.
mcqs.explanation_peer: For a right rotation, the left child goes up and the old root goes down right.

mcqs.question: Which statement about deletion in AVL trees is true?
options: Deletion never causes imbalance.
Deletion may require rotations at multiple ancestors.
Deletion always restores balance with exactly one rotation.
Deletion changes balance factors but never changes subtree heights.
mcqs.answer: Deletion may require rotations at multiple ancestors.
mcqs.hint_teacher: Compare how insertion changes one subtree height versus how deletion can shrink a subtree and affect many ancestors.
mcqs.hint_peer: Deleting is messier than inserting because the height change can ripple upward.
mcqs.explanation_teacher: After deletion, heights may change along the path from the removed node to the root. Multiple ancestors can become imbalanced, so AVL deletion may require rebalancing at several levels.
mcqs.explanation_peer: One delete can make several ancestors wobble.

mcqs.question: If an AVL implementation stores no height field, what must it compute after updates?
options: The key order of the entire tree.
Subtree heights by traversal, unless cached elsewhere.
Only the number of leaves.
The parent pointer for every node.
mcqs.answer: Subtree heights by traversal, unless cached elsewhere.
mcqs.hint_teacher: Balance factors depend on subtree heights.
mcqs.hint_peer: No height field means you have to ask the tree how tall each side is.
mcqs.explanation_teacher: AVL rebalancing requires balance factors, which are computed from subtree heights. Without storing height or balance information, the implementation must recompute heights by traversing subtrees, which increases time cost.
mcqs.explanation_peer: You can skip the height field, but you cannot skip knowing heights somehow.

mcqs.question: When duplicate keys are inserted, which design choice preserves AVL correctness most directly?
options: Ignore duplicates or store a count/list at the node while preserving BST ordering.
Place duplicates arbitrarily in both subtrees.
Make duplicate keys always larger than every key.
Store duplicates only in leaves regardless of key order.
mcqs.answer: Ignore duplicates or store a count/list at the node while preserving BST ordering.
mcqs.hint_teacher: The BST ordering invariant must remain unambiguous.
mcqs.hint_peer: Do not scatter equal keys wherever you want; keep the tree rules clean.
mcqs.explanation_teacher: An AVL tree is also a BST, so duplicate handling must preserve a consistent ordering rule. Common choices are ignoring duplicates, storing a frequency count, or storing a list of equal keys at the existing node.
mcqs.explanation_peer: Equal keys need a home, but they should not break the BST layout.

mcqs.question: Which sequence of keys inserted into an initially empty AVL tree first requires a single left rotation?
mcqs.hint_teacher: A single left rotation fixes an RR imbalance.
mcqs.hint_peer: Insert increasing keys and the right side gets too long.
mcqs.explanation_teacher: Inserting 10, 20, 30 creates a right-right imbalance at node 10. The fix is a single left rotation around 10. The sequence 30, 20, 10 requires a single right rotation, while 10, 30, 20 requires a right-left double rotation.
mcqs.explanation_peer: 10, 20, 30 makes a straight line to the right, so rotate left.

mcqs.question: What is the primary space overhead of a standard AVL node compared with a plain BST node?
options: A hash table.
A height or balance-factor field.
An adjacency matrix.
A priority queue.
mcqs.hint_teacher: AVL decisions are based on local height information.
mcqs.hint_peer: Each node needs a tiny memory note saying how tall its branches are.
mcqs.explanation_teacher: A standard AVL node commonly stores key, left child, right child, and height or balance factor. This extra field enables O(1) local balance checks and O(log n) update operations.
mcqs.explanation_peer: AVL pays one small field per node to stay balanced fast.

mcqs.question: Which property guarantees that an AVL tree's height is O(log n)?
options: Each node has a parent pointer.
The minimum subtree size grows at least like a Fibonacci recurrence.
The tree stores keys in an array.
Every node has exactly two children.
mcqs.answer: The minimum subtree size grows at least like a Fibonacci recurrence.
mcqs.hint_teacher: Use the minimum-node recurrence for AVL trees to derive the height bound.
mcqs.hint_peer: AVL trees cannot stay skinny forever; their smallest possible size grows fast with height.
mcqs.explanation_teacher: Because an AVL tree of height h must contain at least 1+N(h-1)+N(h-2) nodes, the minimum size grows exponentially with h. Inverting that relationship gives h=O(log n).
mcqs.explanation_peer: The tree is not allowed to get too skinny, so height stays logarithmic.

coding_problems.title: Validate AVL Tree
coding_problems.statement: Given the root of a binary tree where each node has key, left, and right, determine whether it is an AVL tree. The tree must satisfy the binary-search-tree ordering property and every node's left and right subtree heights must differ by at most 1. Assume height(null)=0.

examples.explanation: BST order holds and every node has balance factor 0.
BST order fails because 2 appears in the left subtree of 1, and several nodes are not height-balanced.

constraints: Recursion depth may be large; use an iterative approach or increase recursion limit if using recursion.
coding_problems.hint1_teacher: Validate the BST ordering property and the AVL height-balance property separately.
coding_problems.hint1_peer: First ask: are the keys in the right places? Then ask: are the branches too uneven?
coding_problems.hint2_teacher: A node is AVL-valid only if its left and right subtrees are AVL-valid and its balance factor is in [-1, 0, 1].
coding_problems.hint2_peer: Every node needs a local height check, not just the root.

solution_regular.approach: Compute height for each node and validate BST ordering separately. Return false if any balance factor is outside [-1, 0, 1].
solution_regular.time: O(n^2) worst case on skewed trees; O(n log n) on balanced trees.
solution_regular.space: O(h) recursion stack, where h is tree height.

solution_optimal.approach: Traverse once, validating BST ranges and computing subtree heights together. A node is invalid if its key range is violated or its balance factor is outside [-1, 0, 1].
solution_optimal.space: O(n) for the height map; O(h) for the iterative stack.

coding_problems.title: AVL Insertions and Level Order
coding_problems.statement: Given a list of integer keys, insert them into an initially empty AVL tree. If a key already exists, ignore it. Return the level-order traversal of the final AVL tree.

examples.explanation: Inserting 10, 20, 30 triggers a left rotation; later insertions trigger rotations that leave the shown AVL shape.
The duplicate key 5 is ignored, and the remaining keys form a balanced BST.

constraints: Return keys in level-order from left to right at each depth.
coding_problems.hint1_teacher: Use recursive insertion to locate the node, update height, then rebalance using balance factors on the return path.
coding_problems.hint1_peer: Do the normal BST insert, then fix the first wobbly ancestor with the right rotation combo.
coding_problems.hint2_teacher: Classify imbalance as LL, RR, LR, or RL and apply single or double rotations accordingly.
coding_problems.hint2_peer: Left-heavy left child means right rotate; left-heavy right child means left-right double rotate.

solution_regular.approach: Implement AVL insertion without caching height in nodes. Heights are recomputed from subtrees whenever balance factors are needed, which is simple and correct but slower.
solution_regular.time: O(n^2) worst case for n insertions because heights are recomputed repeatedly.
solution_regular.space: O(h) recursion stack plus O(w) traversal queue, where w is maximum width.

solution_optimal.approach: Store height in each node. After each insertion, update heights along the recursion return path and perform at most the necessary AVL rotations.
solution_optimal.time: O(n log n) for n insertions.
solution_optimal.space: O(n) for nodes plus O(log n) recursion stack; O(w) temporary queue during level-order traversal.
